The Union government’s responses to statistical findings reveal an inability to accept hard truths Even as the Union government suggests that there were prima facie reasons for the suspension of the Director of the International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS), K.S. James — the IIPS prepares the National Family Health Surveys (NFHS) and reports to the Health Ministry — it is difficult not to spot vindictive motives. In recent years, the government has taken a hostile approach towards the release of any data, even by its own agencies, that reveal inconvenient truths about its policies and their outcomes, rather than using them as feedback. The NFHS-5 (2019-21), for example, debunked the government’s claim in 2019 that all villages were open defecation free (ODF); it showed that 19% of surveyed households did not use any toilet facility. Other surveys, i.e., the National Statistical Office survey from October 2018, the National Annual Rural Sanitation Survey of 2019-20 and the Multiple Indicator Survey released earlier this year, also indicated that many villages were not ODF. The NFHS-5 also showed a rise in anaemia and that 57% of the surveyed rural households lacked access to LPG or natural gas, calling into question the impact of the Ujjwala Yojana. What transpired in the recent past with other statistical findings is also revealing. The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation had junked its consumer expenditure survey (CES) of 2017-18 ostensibly due to data quality concerns even as important indices related to inflation and poverty continue to be pegged to the CES of 2011-12. The NSSO’s Periodic Labour Force Survey, which was cleared by the National Statistical Commission (NSC) in 2018, was held back for showing a sharp increase in unemployment, but was released only after the government returned to power in 2019. The delay resulted in the resignations of the former acting chairman and another member of the NSC over the interference of the NITI Aayog in statistical issues. NITI Aayog’s involvement in releasing the back series on GDP growth that contradicted an NSC report in 2018, was another indication of the government’s efforts to undermine traditional statistical institutions. Recently, a series of opinion articles by members of the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister sought to discredit the methodology used by the NFHS and similar surveys. The government has also unduly and unjustifiably delayed the decennial Census exercise, putting into limbo several statistical measures and programmes dependent upon Census information. questions.question: Comprehension: Read the following passage and answer the questions given after it . Horace Danby was perceived as a model citizen. A man in his fifties, living with a health-conscious housekeeper, he was a successful locksmith. However, there was a hidden side to Horace. He harbored a passion for rare books and to fund his obsession, he had committed a theft annually for fifteen years. It was a sunlit July afternoon when Horace approached Shotover Grange, a mansion he had been observing for two weeks. He knew the family was away and the only two servants were out watching a movie. With precision, Horace intended to rob the Grange's safe containing £15,000 worth of jewels to buy three rare books that had caught his eye. Finding the key to the kitchen door outside, he entered and was met by a small dog, Sherry. Horace, knowing the dog's name, kept him calm. With the servants absent for four more hours, he made his way to the safe behind a mediocre painting in the drawing room. As he set his tools and prepared to break in, the scent of fresh flowers overwhelmed his senses, triggering his hay fever. Just then, a feminine voice queried if he had a cold. Startled, Horace found a young, elegantly dressed woman in the doorway. She was calm and poised, suggesting that he see a doctor for his hay fever. As they spoke, it became evident that she was part of the household. Trying to save the situation, Horace subtly threatened her, but the woman remained unflappable. She proposed a deal: in exchange for her silence, Horace would crack the safe for her. She explained she had forgotten the combination but needed her jewels for a party. Seizing the opportunity, Horace agreed. Within an hour, Horace had retrieved the jewels for the woman, believing he had gained an ally and an escape from potential imprisonment. For two days, he refrained from any criminal activity, honoring his commitment. However, the allure of the rare books beckoned, making him contemplate his next theft. To Horace's shock, he was arrested for the robbery at Shotover Grange. His fingerprints, discovered all over the room where he had worked without gloves, betrayed him. He pleaded his case, citing the young woman's request, but faced disbelief. The owner's wife, a stern, elderly woman, denied any involvement, sealing Horace's fate. In prison, Horace assumed the role of assistant librarian. He often found himself ruminating over the charming young imposter who had outsmarted him, realizing that she too was a thief. The age-old saying 'honour among thieves' now irked him, given his bitter experience. Q42. What was the reason behind Horace Danby's annual thefts ?
